resources.headline: Partner Ecosystems Earned Their Strategic Seat At The Table — Now What?
resources.fullText: < Featured Blogs Home > Featured Blogs > Partner Ecosystems Earned Their Strategic Seat At The Table — Now What? Partner Ecosystems Earned Their Strategic Seat At The Table — Now What? Partner Ecosystem Strategy Is Business Strategy For years, B2B partner ecosystem leaders have worked to prove that partner ecosystems deserve strategic attention. Our latest survey data suggests that this battle has largely been won. According to The State Of B2B Partner Ecosystems, 2026, 70% of partner ecosystem and channel marketing decision-makers say that orchestrating or optimizing a partner ecosystem is very important or absolutely essential to their organization. The Business Impact Is Difficult To Ignore Why the heightened attention? The growing importance of partner ecosystems is not simply a matter of executive perception. It is grounded in measurable business impact. Nearly 60% of respondents to our survey reported that over 40% of their organization’s revenue is attributable to partners and indirect routes to market. This finding also underscores a significant shift in how organizations create value. Partner ecosystems are not merely generating resell transactions. Our research reveals that partner ecosystems are going further by helping B2B providers drive innovation, extend their offering portfolios, expand market reach, support buyers throughout increasingly complex purchasing journeys, provide specialized expertise, and contribute to revenue outcomes in ways that extend beyond traditional channel models. As partner ecosystems expand and mature, their influence increasingly spans both indirect and direct revenue opportunities. But despite the now widespread recognition of the importance and value of partner ecosystems, a critical gap remains. The Greatest Risk Is Underinvestment When asked about the biggest barriers to partner ecosystem success, 50% of respondents identified a lack of resources as a top challenge. While supplier organizations increasingly understand the value of partner ecosystems, many have yet to make the investments necessary to fully capitalize on them. The implications are significant. As buyers increasingly evaluate the strength of a provider’s ecosystem alongside its products and services, expanded investment in the people, leadership, and capabilities to orchestrate partner ecosystems effectively will drive greater growth and create differentiated customer value. The question is no longer whether partner ecosystems matter but whether organizations are investing in them at a level that matches their strategic importance. Closing The Partner Ecosystem Investment Gap If your organization views partner ecosystems as essential to growth, innovation, revenue generation, customer value, and competitive differentiation, now is the time to assess whether your partner ecosystem investments align with those expectations. Evaluate the resources, skills, leadership, and operational support required for your partner ecosystem initiatives and identify gaps that could limit future success. To learn more about expected partner ecosystem growth, revenue trends, and the challenges that supplier organizations must address to maximize value, read The State Of B2B Partner Ecosystems, 2026 and reach out to schedule an inquiry or guidance session. keyNotes: It turns out that working with other businesses (called "partner ecosystems") is now seen as a crucial part of a company's overall strategy. A recent survey showed that 70% of leaders believe managing these partnerships is extremely important for their organization.
These partnerships aren't just for show; they significantly boost a company's earnings. Almost 60% of companies reported that over 40% of their total income comes from these business partners.

What's surprising is that these partners do much more than just help sell products. They also play a big role in helping companies create new things, expand their offerings, reach more customers, and provide expert advice.

Despite how valuable these partnerships are, many companies aren't investing enough in them. A major challenge for 50% of companies is simply not having enough money or staff to properly support their partner efforts.
resources.question: The article highlights that business partners (or "partner ecosystems") contribute significantly to a company's revenue and do much more than just sell products, like helping with new ideas and reaching customers. Thinking about your own work or industry, what kinds of partnerships could you explore that might unlock new value or solve problems in ways you haven't considered before, beyond just traditional sales?

resources.headline: Has Your Partner Demand Strategy Kept Up With Your Evolving Partner Ecosystem?
resources.fullText: < Featured Blogs Home > Featured Blogs > Has Your Partner Demand Strategy Kept Up With Your Evolving Partner Ecosystem? Has Your Partner Demand Strategy Kept Up With Your Evolving Partner Ecosystem? B2B partner ecosystems are becoming larger, more diverse, and more complex, yet some organizations continue to apply an outdated, single partner demand strategy across fundamentally different partner business models. The consequences are clear: Investments are misaligned, resources are spread inefficiently, partner engagement suffers, and demand performance falls short of expectations — the opposite of driving efficient growth with partners. The need for change is already evident. According to Forrester’s Partner Ecosystem Marketing Survey, 2026, 70% of partner ecosystem marketing decision-makers plan to update their partner demand strategy within the next 12 months. Simply put, many partner demand strategies have failed to evolve alongside the partner ecosystems that they are intended to support. Thankfully, most decision-makers recognize the need for change. Different Partners Require Different Demand Strategies Different partners create value differently. They follow different routes to market, bring distinct offerings to buyers, hold varying levels of demand influence, and possess widely different marketing capabilities. Yet many partner demand strategies continue to overlook these differences. A strategy designed for one partner can be ineffective, or even counterproductive, when applied to another. The answer is better alignment: Ensure that partner demand strategies are intentionally aligned to how each partner creates value and brings offerings to market. Retire One-Size-Fits-All Approaches To Partner Demand More funding, more programs, and more partner demand activities will not solve a strategy built on outdated assumptions. The Forrester Ecosystem-Aligned Partner Demand Strategy Framework provides a blueprint for closing that gap. By applying the seven keys in the framework, partner ecosystem marketing leaders can move beyond one-size-fits-all approaches and build partner demand strategies tailored to unlock the realities of their unique partner ecosystem. The longer organizations wait, the greater the misalignment, wasted investment, and gap between partner ecosystem opportunity and partner demand performance. Is Your Partner Demand Strategy Keeping Pace With Your Partner Ecosystem? If your partner ecosystem has expanded in size, diversity, or complexity over the past several years, ask yourself a simple question: Has your partner demand strategy evolved along with it? For many organizations, the answer is no. That needs to change. Read Forrester’s report, Implementing The Ecosystem-Aligned Partner Demand Strategy Framework, and start modernizing your partner demand strategies before today’s alignment gap becomes tomorrow’s growth challenge. Forrester clients can reach out to schedule a guidance session with me to apply this research to your specific partner ecosystem. keyNotes: It's surprising that many companies still use a single, old-fashioned marketing plan for all their business partners, even though these partners are very diverse. This leads to wasted money, unhappy partners, and poor results.

A big change is coming: 70% of leaders responsible for marketing with business partners plan to update their marketing plans for these partners within the next year. This shows many realize their current approach isn't working.

The article highlights that a marketing plan designed for one type of business partner can actually be ineffective or even harmful when applied to another. This is because different partners create value and reach customers in very different ways.

Simply adding more money or programs won't fix the problem; instead, companies need to create specific marketing plans that are carefully matched to how each business partner creates value and sells products.
resources.question: The article emphasizes that a "one-size-fits-all" approach to working with partners often fails because each partner is unique. Where in your own work or relationships do you currently use a single approach for different situations, and how might tailoring your strategy to each specific case lead to better outcomes?

resources.fullText: If you manage complex dealer networks, you know that legacy technologies can limit both your team and your buyers. As a leading manufacturer of engines and parts for lawn, landscape, and other commercial…
keyNotes: Kawasaki Engines managed to bring in an extra $6.5 million in just 90 days, showing how quickly improvements in how a business operates can lead to big financial gains.
A major challenge for Kawasaki Engines was their 'legacy technologies,' which are just old computer systems that made it hard for both their own employees and their customers to get things done.
Kawasaki Engines makes parts like engines for things you see every day, such as lawnmowers and other commercial equipment, highlighting that even behind-the-scenes businesses can make a huge impact.
The article points out that managing 'complex dealer networks' – essentially, a lot of different businesses that sell Kawasaki's products for them – can be tricky with outdated systems.
resources.question: The article mentions that 'legacy technologies' (old computer systems) limited both Kawasaki's team and their buyers. In your own work or business, what 'legacy' way of doing things, whether it's a tool or a process, might be holding back your team or your customers, and what's one small change you could explore to improve it?

topicB.name: B2B Marketing Strategy and AI Transformation

resources.headline: B2B Marketers Hand AI Execution And Keep The Strategy, Survey Finds
resources.fullText: A survey reveals that B2B marketing leaders primarily view AI as an execution tool, retaining strategic oversight themselves.
keyNotes: A recent study found that people leading marketing teams in companies that sell to other businesses mostly see artificial intelligence (AI) as a tool to help them *do* tasks.
These marketing leaders are making sure they keep control over the big picture planning and direction for their marketing efforts, rather than letting AI decide this.
Essentially, the survey shows that humans are holding onto the 'thinking' part of marketing, which is called strategy, while giving the 'doing' part, or execution, to AI.
This means that for marketing, the human leaders are still the ones making the important decisions about what to achieve, and AI is used to carry out those plans.
resources.question: The article highlights that marketing leaders are giving AI the 'execution' tasks but keeping the 'strategic oversight' for themselves. In your own work, what specific parts of your job would you consider 'execution' that you'd happily hand over to a smart tool, and what 'strategic oversight' would you never give up?

resources.headline: The Preference Marketing Matrix: A Model For Fueling Brand And Demand Growth
resources.fullText: The Preference Marketing Matrix: A Model For Fueling Brand And Demand Growth  Forrester
keyNotes: The article introduces a concept called the "Preference Marketing Matrix," which is presented as a specific way of thinking about how companies do their marketing.
This "Matrix" is designed to help businesses achieve two main goals: making their company more recognized and liked, which the article calls "brand growth."
The other key goal of this approach is to increase the number of people who want and buy a company's products or services, referred to as "demand growth."
According to the article from Forrester, this "Matrix" is a model intended to help businesses grow both their reputation and their customer base.
resources.question: The article title suggests a 'Preference Marketing Matrix' helps grow a company's reputation and customer interest. Without knowing the details of this specific matrix, what aspects of your own business do you think currently make customers genuinely prefer you over competitors, and how might you intentionally strengthen those preferences?

resources.headline: Go-to-Market Strategy in 2026: How to Launch, Grow, and Scale Your Business
resources.fullText: Launching a successful business, product, or service takes more than a great idea. You need to understand your market, reach the right customers, communicate your value, and build the systems that support sustainable growth. That is where a go-to-market (GTM) strategy comes in. Whether you are introducing your first product, expanding into a new market, or launching a digital service, your go-to-market strategy determines how effectively you turn ambition into opportunity. At Mathenge Inc., we believe successful businesses are strategically positioned, thoughtfully built, and continuously improved. This guide explains what a go-to-market strategy is, why it matters, and how to build one that supports measurable growth. What is a go-to-market strategy? A go-to-market strategy is a structured plan for introducing a product or service to its target customers, establishing a competitive position, and generating demand and sales. It answers five questions: Who are we targeting? What problem are we solving? Why should customers choose us? How will we reach and convert customers? How will we measure success? An effective GTM strategy connects product development, branding, marketing, sales, technology, and customer experience. The goal is to introduce the right offering to the right audience through the right channels, with the ability to learn and adapt. Why every growing business needs a GTM strategy Businesses often build a product, website, or advertising campaign before establishing who their customers are and why those customers should buy. Without alignment, they may experience low visibility, unqualified leads, websites that do not convert, disconnected workflows, and unclear performance metrics. A well-developed GTM strategy connects business objectives with practical execution. It is especially valuable for companies entering new markets or launching innovative products. The eight essential steps 1. Understand your market and ideal customer Begin with research into your industry, competitive landscape, and target audience. Ask who benefits most, what challenges they face, how they solve them today, and what influences their decisions. Build an ideal customer profile describing your best-fit customer or organisation. For B2B businesses this may include company size, industry, location, budget, and decision-makers. For B2C businesses, behaviour, preferences, and purchasing motivations may be more relevant. 2. Develop a clear value proposition and brand positioning Your value proposition explains why customers should choose you over alternatives. Focus on the customer’s desired outcome rather than simply listing features. For example, “We develop websites and software” is less meaningful than “We build connected digital experiences and business systems that help companies attract customers, operate efficiently, and grow.” Strong positioning needs consistent messaging and a recognisable visual identity. Mathenge Inc.’s Brand Identity & Strategy solutions help organisations communicate their value clearly. 3. Create a digital foundation that supports growth Your GTM strategy is only as strong as the infrastructure supporting it. A growth-ready foundation may include a responsive SEO-ready website, landing pages, CRM workflows, analytics, secure portals, payments, and automated communication. Mathenge Inc. builds Websites & Digital Experiences, custom software, and connected systems around real business needs. The objective is digital infrastructure that supports today’s operations and tomorrow’s growth. 4. Build a digital marketing and acquisition strategy Choose channels based on where your customers spend time and how they make decisions. Search engine optimisation improves discoverability, content marketing builds trust, social media supports awareness, paid advertising creates targeted reach, and email nurtures relationships. The best approach is not to use every channel. It is to choose the right combination for your audience, resources, and objectives. Our Digital Marketing & Growth services connect strategy, content, search, campaigns, and performance insights. 5. Align sales with the customer journey A typical journey moves from awareness to consideration, enquiry, consultation, proposal, purchase, and retention. Each stage needs a different experience: education early on, proof and clarity during evaluation, and strong onboarding after purchase. When marketing and sales are aligned, teams reduce confusion, improve follow-up, and create a more consistent customer experience. 6. Use AI and automation to improve efficiency AI adoption should begin with a business problem, not a desire to use the newest tool. Practical applications include lead qualification, enquiry routing, customer support, reporting, research, and connected business workflows. Through AI Automation & Workflows, Mathenge Inc. helps organisations reduce repetitive work and improve operations. Technology should support your strategy, not complicate it. 7. Set clear KPIs and measure performance Define success before launch. Useful measures include website traffic, conversion rate, customer acquisition cost, qualified leads, customer lifetime value, revenue growth, and retention. The right metrics depend on your model. A software startup may prioritise activation and retention, while a professional services firm may focus on qualified enquiries, consultation bookings, and proposal conversion. Our Data, Analytics & Intelligence solutions help teams turn performance data into useful decisions. 8. Launch, learn, and continuously improve A GTM strategy does not end on launch day. Run a controlled pilot where possible, monitor customer responses, identify friction, and improve the offer, message, and customer journey. Your strategy should evolve as customers, competitors, and objectives change. Go-to-market strategy versus marketing strategy A GTM strategy focuses on introducing an offering or entering a market.
